lead: Energy crosses a system's boundary in two ways other than with flowing mass: as heat, driven by a temperature difference, and as work, every other kind of transfer, such as a moving piston, a turning shaft or an electric current. Neither is stored in the system; both exist only while they cross the boundary, and both depend on the path. Because energy can cross in either direction, every calculation must start with a sign convention. This book takes heat into the system as positive and work done by the system as positive, the usual engineering choice, since an engine's useful output then comes out positive.

blocks.text: In mechanics, work is a force moving through a distance, W = ∫F dx. Thermodynamics needs a definition that covers shafts and wires too: work is done by a system on its surroundings if the sole effect on everything outside the system could have been the raising of a weight. A turbine shaft could wind up a rope and lift a load; a battery could drive a motor that does the same. Neither is literally lifting a weight, but each could, so each is work.

Heat is energy that crosses the boundary because of a temperature difference between the system and its surroundings, from the hotter to the colder side. A cup of tea cooling in a room loses heat; once both are at the same temperature, heat transfer stops. Words such as 'the heat in the tea' are loose: the tea has internal energy, and heat is only the name of the transfer.

Both are measured in joules (kJ in most problems). Their rates are in watts: heat rate Q̇ in kW and power Ẇ in kW, with 1 kW = 1 kJ/s. Small amounts are written δQ and δW, not dQ and dW, because they are inexact differentials: ∫δW from state 1 to state 2 is W₁₂, the work of that path, not W₂ − W₁, since a system has no 'work at state 2'.

Positive when

blocks.text: So 'heat rejected is 30 kJ' becomes Q = −30 kJ, and 'work done on the gas is 40 kJ' becomes W = −40 kJ. The net energy delivered to the system by these two transfers is Q − W; the first law turns that into a change of the system's energy.
Net energy in by heat and work = Q − W
blocks.where: Q and W are signed as in the table, in kJ. Some textbooks, and most chemistry books, count work done on the system as positive and write Q + W instead; both describe the same physics. State the convention at the top of every answer and do not switch half way.

sections.h3: Adiabatic and diathermic boundaries; heat and work compared

blocks.text: An adiabatic boundary allows no heat transfer, Q = 0, though work can cross it; a thick lagged steam pipe or a vacuum flask comes close. A diathermic boundary allows heat transfer, but does not force it: a metal wall between two regions at the same temperature carries no heat. Adiabatic is not isolated: an isolated system also has W = 0 and no mass crossing.

head: Heat
Work
rows: any other cause: force, torque, voltage
Can be fully converted to the other?
yes, by friction or a resistor

blocks.text: Heat and work are alike in that both are boundary phenomena, both are path functions and both are measured in joules. They differ in what drives them, and in quality: work can always be turned completely into heat, but heat cannot be turned completely into work in a cycle, which is the subject of the second law.

sections.h3: The boundary decides which is which

blocks.text: Whether a transfer is heat or work depends on where the boundary is drawn. An electric heater immersed in a gas is the clearest case. If the boundary includes the heater, electricity crosses the boundary through the wire: that is electrical work done on the system. If the boundary encloses only the gas and leaves the heater outside, the hot heater surface warms the gas across a temperature difference: that is heat. The numbers change labels, but the net energy received is the same (Figure 1.6.1). Draw the boundary, then name each transfer.

examples.question: Gas in a cylinder is warmed by an electric heater of 0.50 kW inside the cylinder, switched on for 2.0 minutes. Meanwhile the gas pushes the piston out, doing 25 kJ of work, and 15 kJ of heat leaks through the cylinder wall to the room. Using Q > 0 into the system and W > 0 out of it, find Q, W and Q − W (a) for a boundary that includes the heater, and (b) for a boundary around the gas only. (c) Write the result of (a) in the convention where work on the system is positive.
steps: Energy from the heater: 0.50 kW × (2.0 × 60) s = 0.50 kJ/s × 120 s = 60 kJ.
(a) The heater is inside the boundary, so its 60 kJ enters through the wire as electrical work done on the system, −60 kJ. The piston work is done by the system, +25 kJ. Total W = 25 − 60 = −35 kJ.
The only heat crossing this boundary is the leak to the room: Q = −15 kJ.
Q − W = −15 − (−35) = +20 kJ: a net 20 kJ enters the system.
(b) The heater is outside the boundary. It is hotter than the gas, so its 60 kJ crosses as heat into the gas: Q = +60 − 15 = +45 kJ. The only work is at the piston: W = +25 kJ.
Q − W = 45 − 25 = +20 kJ, the same net energy as in (a).
(c) With work on the system counted positive, the heater work is +60 kJ and the piston work is −25 kJ, so W′ = +35 kJ, while Q = −15 kJ as before. Net energy in = Q + W′ = −15 + 35 = +20 kJ.
examples.answer: (a) Q = −15 kJ, W = −35 kJ, Q − W = +20 kJ. (b) Q = +45 kJ, W = +25 kJ, Q − W = +20 kJ. (c) Q = −15 kJ, W′ = +35 kJ, Q + W′ = +20 kJ. The labels depend on the boundary and the convention; the net energy does not.

traps: 'Heat rejected 30 kJ' is Q = −30 kJ, and 'work done on the system 40 kJ' is W = −40 kJ in this book's convention. Writing them positive flips the answer.
Do not mix conventions: Q − W goes with W positive out of the system; Q + W goes with W positive into the system.
An electric heater inside the boundary gives work, not heat. Only when the boundary leaves the heater out does its energy cross as heat.
Adiabatic means Q = 0 only. Work can still cross an adiabatic boundary, so an adiabatic system is not automatically isolated.
δW and δQ are inexact: write W₁₂, never W₂ − W₁.

quiz.q: State the sign convention for Q and W used in this book.
quiz.a: Q is positive when heat enters the system; W is positive when the system does work on the surroundings.

quiz.q: Give the thermodynamic definition of work.
quiz.a: Work is done by a system if the sole effect on everything outside it could be the raising of a weight.

quiz.q: Give two similarities and two differences between heat and work.
quiz.a: Similar: both are boundary phenomena that exist only during a process, and both are path functions. Different: heat is driven by a temperature difference and work by any other cause; work converts fully into heat, but heat cannot convert fully into work in a cycle.

quiz.q: Does a diathermic wall always transfer heat? Explain.
quiz.a: No. It allows heat transfer, but heat flows only if there is a temperature difference across it; at equal temperatures Q = 0.

quiz.q: A system rejects 25 kJ of heat and has 10 kJ of work done on it. Write Q and W and find Q − W.
quiz.a: Q = −25 kJ, W = −10 kJ, Q − W = −25 + 10 = −15 kJ: the system's energy falls by 15 kJ.

quiz.q: A 2.0 kW electric kettle runs for 3 minutes. Taking the kettle element and water together as the system, find W.
quiz.a: Energy = 2.0 kJ/s × 180 s = 360 kJ, entering through the cord as electrical work on the system: W = −360 kJ.

quiz.q: A gas in an adiabatic cylinder is stirred by a paddle wheel. A student writes Q = +50 kJ for the stirring energy. Correct the answer.
quiz.a: The boundary is adiabatic, so Q = 0. The paddle shaft crosses the boundary, so the stirring energy is shaft work done on the gas: W = −50 kJ.

quiz.q: Why do different boundaries in the worked example give different Q and W but the same Q − W?
quiz.a: Moving the boundary changes how the heater's 60 kJ is classified (work through the wire, or heat from a hot surface), but it is the same 60 kJ entering the gas. Since both routes deliver it, the net energy received, Q − W = +20 kJ, does not change.

beyond: Process-simulation software reports heat duties with signs (a negative duty is cooling), and test standards for engines and pumps state which side of the boundary each meter sits on. Exergy analysis gives heat a lower value than work, because heat at low temperature can produce little work.
